Daniel / team —

Attaching our raw test artifacts and a short technical note. Key points up front:

- Test harness: open-source harness based on a modified Hellman load generator (configured here) + replay of a 60/20/20 prompt length distribution (short/medium/long). Warm-up policy: 120s prefix warm-up per model + one KV-cache priming pass (for chat use-cases).
- Workload mix: 60% short (avg 75 tokens), 30% medium (avg 200 tokens), 10% long (avg 600 tokens). This aligns with typical enterprise chat+generation mixes.
- Concurrency sweep: we ran steady-state ramps at 10, 50, 200, 800 concurrent requests for the same model variant. Observed p50/p95/p99/p999 (attached CSVs):
  • 10 concurrent: p50=38ms, p95=82ms, p99=145ms, p999=398ms
  • 50 concurrent: p50=42ms, p95=96ms, p99=176ms, p999=590ms
  • 200 concurrent: p50=60ms, p95=150ms, p99=420ms, p999=1.8s
  • 800 concurrent: p50=120ms, p95=420ms, p99=1.6s, p999=6.1s (note: this level triggers saturation on a single GPU pool)
- Burst & saturation: saturation modes are driven by continuous-batching queues and KV-cache eviction. At saturation we see a bi-modal tail: a fast path for batched requests and a slower path where requests wait for new kernel invocations.
- Mitigations we use: adaptive pre-batching thresholds, short-prefork worker pools for very low-latency requests, and dynamic fallback to quantized model variants.
- Backoff/retry guidance: prefer client-side jittered exponential backoff with a 50–200ms base for P95-sensitive APIs; server-side 503s include Retry-After when we trigger queue-shed.

Attachments included: scaling-results-20270401.csv, latency-percentiles-graphs.png. CSVs include columns: timestamp, concurrency_level, qps, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, p999_ms, avg_tokens, model_variant.

Notes on hosted vs dedicated/private:
- Hosted: auto-scaling and dynamic batching give best cost/latency for bursty workloads; cross-region fallback is automatic for accounts with regional failover enabled.
- Dedicated: consistent pool sizing reduces p999 variance at the cost of headroom; no cross-tenant autoscaling unless configured in your dedicated contract.
- Private/on-prem: behavior depends on customer infra; we provide identical runtime and a recommended config for batching and pre-fork options.

Happy to jump on a 30-min call to walk through the CSVs.

—Vivek
Vivek Kulkarni
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime — Redwood Inference

Daniel —

Thanks Vivek — attached is a concise 1-page executive summary tailored for procurement and SRE reviewers. Highlights below:

- Recommended SLA bands:
  • Standard: 99.9% availability, p95 < 250ms for short/medium blends at committed QPS
  • Premium (dedicated): 99.95% availability, p99 < 500ms with reserved headroom
- Capacity tiers & pricing implication: we document soft/firm capacity tiers in the attached CSV. For sustained 200+ concurrent requests we recommend a Dedicated pool to reduce tail variance.
- Fallback pattern we propose for Globex:
  1) Primary hosted pool in us-east with auto-scale. 2) Canary to quantized model for heavy bursts (quality trade-off documented). 3) Cross-region failover to us-west for regional failures. 4) Graceful degradation: return partial output with structured fallback (indicate model_version: degraded) when latencies exceed configured SLO.
- Procurement artifacts included: sample SLA language, suggested CAN/FAILover testing cadence, and a short checklist for your SREs to validate before go-live.

We can include a sample DocuSign or contract redline if you’d like — looping in Neha for pricing and commercial language.

Best,
Monica Patel
